newsitem.title: UK: Rise in temp jobs to unsettle UK workers - report.
newsitem.headline: Rise in temp jobs to unsettle UK workers - report.

text.p: Temporary employment in the UK, expected to increase in the future, may prompt greater worker dissatisfaction, according to a new report on Monday.
The London Chamber of Commerce and Industry said in its labour market briefing "Atypical employment in the capital", that 38 percent of temporary employees would prefer a permanent position.
"Although only seven percent of employees nationwide are presently working under temporary contracts, a major expansion of this form of employment may increase worker dissatisfaction," it said.
Atypical employment -- such as part-time work and temporary and self employment -- can reduce firms' costs and increase their ability to react to fluctuations in aggregate and product demand.

The government has claimed credit for an increasingly flexible labour force in Britain by introducing deregulatory policies, the LCC said. Opposition MPs have countered that labour market deregulation generates only low-skill, insecure jobs.
The LCC said some academics argued that the changes indentified by both sides of the political debate are the result of long-term structural changes rather than deregulation.

It said Peter Robinson of the London School of Economics' Centre for Economic Performance argued there is little evidence of a significant reduction in job tenure and only trends in self-employment seem to have been significantly altered since 1979.
"Growth in part-time employment was stronger in the 1950s and 1960s than in the 1980s, whilst temporary employment still only accounts for seven percent of employees," the LCC said.
